acceptedAnswer.text:
Composition in photography is how the elements within a frame

relate to one another. Your viewpoint, framing, timing and use

of space influence what a viewer notices and how the photograph

feels. Composition begins with recognising what interests you,

then making choices that help express it.

mainEntity.name: What makes a good photography composition?

acceptedAnswer.text:
A good composition supports what the photograph is trying to

communicate. The placement of elements, light, space and visual

weight contribute to its meaning or feeling. A photograph can

work through simplicity, complexity, stability or tension.

Judge those choices by their effect on the actual image rather

than how closely they follow a grid.

mainEntity.name: What are the seven rules of composition in photography?

acceptedAnswer.text:
There is no single agreed list of seven composition rules.

Seven commonly taught techniques are the rule of thirds,

leading lines, framing, symmetry, balance, negative space and

repetition. Each offers a way to explore a photograph. Use a

technique when it supports your intention, and compare

alternatives rather than treating the list as a checklist.

Explore these tools in

Lesson 26 — Composition Rules .

mainEntity.name: Do you have to follow the rule of thirds?

acceptedAnswer.text:
No. The rule of thirds is an optional guide that divides a

frame into nine equal rectangles and suggests placing important

elements near the dividing lines or their intersections.

Central placement, symmetry or a subject close to an edge may

better express your intention. Compare the alternatives and

consider what each placement contributes.

mainEntity.name: How can beginners improve their photography composition?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Beginners can improve composition by practising one deliberate

choice at a time. Photograph the same scene twice, changing

your position, framing or another compositional decision.

Compare the results and explain which better expresses what

caught your attention. Check the edges and background as well

as the main area of interest. Repeat the exercise with a

specific lesson from your review.

mainEntity.name: What does See, Feel, Technique mean in photography?

acceptedAnswer.text:
SEE → FEEL → TECHNIQUE is the central process in

Alan Ranger’s Composition Framework. See means noticing what

draws your attention. Feel means recognising the response or

meaning you want to preserve. Technique means choosing the

position, framing and camera settings that support it.

You can return to observation whenever the scene or your

understanding changes.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between framing and composition?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Framing concerns the boundaries of the photograph: what you

include, exclude and position within its four edges.

Composition encompasses how all those elements work together,

including their spacing, visual weight and relationships.

A frame within a frame, such as a doorway or branches, is one

optional framing technique.

Lesson 27 — Framing

explores these decisions.

mainEntity.name: How much negative space should a photograph have?

acceptedAnswer.text:
There is no required percentage of negative space in a

photograph. The amount depends on what the space contributes

to the image, such as isolation, scale, stillness or uncertainty.

Compare tighter and more spacious framings, then choose the

relationship that supports your intention. Space can carry

meaning in its own right, as explored in

Lesson 30 — Negative Space .

mainEntity.name: Can you practise photography composition with a phone?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Yes. A phone lets you practise observation, viewpoint, framing,

timing and the relationship between elements. Move closer,

step back or change your angle, then compare how the photograph

changes. Different cameras offer different technical controls,

but you can develop compositional judgement with the camera

you already have.

mainEntity.name: How do you know when a photograph is finished?

acceptedAnswer.text:
A photograph is finished when further changes no longer help

it express what matters to you. Identify what already works,

then compare any proposed adjustment with the original.

Keep changes that serve the photograph and reject those that

weaken it. Feedback can reveal something you missed, while

the final decision remains yours. Continue with

Lesson 34 — Improving Composition .
